results.title: Assessing the Value of Explainable Artificial Intelligence for ...
results.content: To address this issue, the field of eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) aims to clarify the rationale behind AI predictions while ensuring compliance with ethical standards and advanced regulations such as the GDPR and the AI Act. This study applies multiple explainability methods to a diagnostic support model for Distal Myopathies (DMs), a rare neuromuscular disorder marked by subtle, early-stage tissue alterations. However, the existing literature presents several gaps: (1) current explainability methods for MRI-based diagnosis have primarily focused on common diseases with large datasets, with limited attention given to rare conditions such as DMs; (2) existing saliency-based methods often generate noisy, low-resolution explanations that are difficult for clinicians to interpret; and (3) few studies have evaluated the practical clinical relevance of XAI outputs through direct user studies with radiologists. The evaluation of explainability techniques including SHAP, GradCAM, occlusion-based methods, and ensemble approaches revealed no universally superior method.

results.title: Explainable AI-driven MRI-based brain tumor classification - Frontiers
results.content: An automated brain tumor classification in MR images using an enhanced convolutional neural network, Singh and Agarwal (2023) proposes an advanced CNN model that achieves high accuracy in classifying brain tumors using MRI images. Compared to other architectures, such as the 3-conv-128-nodes-2-dense-2-dropout model, which reached a validation accuracy of 92.76%, the additional convolutional layer in this design effectively captured intricate tumor-specific features without introducing significant overfitting. Overall, the strong performance metrics, including high accuracy, low loss, and balanced precision-recall values, demonstrate that the model effectively learns dis-criminative features for brain tumor classification. In the evaluation of various convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures for brain tumor classification (refer to Table 4), the 4-conv-1-dense-1-dropout model emerged as the best-performing model, achieving an accuracy of 95.86%, a remarkably low loss of 0.12, and high precision, recall, and F1-score (all 0.95). Keywords: brain tumor classification, convolutional neural networks, data augmentation, deep learning, explainable AI, feature visualization, medical imaging, MRI.

results.title: Explainable and likelihood aware AI framework for MRI-based pixel ...
results.content: Trained solely on annotated normal bladder MRI scans, ELAAI integrates three novel modules: MFA-Net, a robust multi-scale feature aggregation network for bladder segmentation; a refinement step employing adaptive tolerance technique to enhance segmentation of irregularities; and a single-step likelihood prediction network (SLIP-Net), which is a vision transformer with a novel multi-scale deterministic uncertainty (MSDU) head for tumour likelihood prediction. Unlike prior works that depend on tumour-labelled MRIs, ELAAI learns bladder anatomy from normal scans with MFA-Net, applies adaptive tolerance score-based mask refinement, and then uses SLIP-Net, to convert masked MRI slice-pair registration variability into pixel-wise tumour likelihood. Similar results follow for the MRI scans in rows fourth to seventh of Fig. 4 that demonstrate MFA-Net’s superior segmentation capabilities across diverse bladder morphologies, including asymmetrical, compact, low-contrast, and blurred boundaries. The ELAAI framework offers a novel approach to BT detection by integrating robust segmentation through MFA-Net, knowledge-driven refinement, and pixel-level likelihood prediction via SLIP-Net. Its adaptability to limited annotated data addresses a critical gap, making it particularly impactful for data-scarce medical imaging applications.
